analysis.one_liner: Finances Senate campaigns with small-donor public money instead of large private contributions.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 24, 2019 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it died without a hearing, markup, or vote; 28 of 100 senators cosponsored it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up a Fair Elections Fund that pays Senate candidates who agree to raise money only from small in-state donations of up to $200. Candidates who gather enough small contributions get a lump-sum grant, a 600% match on small donations, and TV ad vouchers, in exchange for giving up large checks, joint fundraising committees, and spending their own money. The fund would be fed in part by a new 0.5% tax on federal payments to companies holding contracts worth more than $10 million.
analysis.who_benefits: Senate candidates who can build support through many small donations, especially challengers and candidates without access to wealthy donor networks, and voters who want candidates answering to constituents rather than large donors.

how_it_helps.text: A candidate who collects qualifying small in-state contributions (at least 2,000 plus 500 per congressional district, each $5–$200 from state residents) becomes a participating candidate eligible for fund money [S3].

Participating candidates receive a base allocation of $750,000 plus $150,000 per congressional district for the general election, a 600% match on qualified small-dollar contributions, and additional enhanced matching payments [S3].
For the general election, participants get broadcast advertising vouchers worth $100,000 per congressional district and pay no more than 80% of the lowest broadcast rate for TV ads [S3].

In exchange, participating candidates may accept only small-dollar contributions and fund payments, no contributions over $200 outside those channels, no personal or family spending on their campaigns, and no joint fundraising committees [S3].
The fund would be supported by a 0.5% tax on payments made under federal contracts worth more than $10 million, capped at $500,000 per contract per year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies holding federal contracts over $10 million would pay the 0.5% fee on contract payments. Large donors and fundraising operations would lose their central role, since participating candidates could not take their money. Taxpayers would cover any shortfall, because the tax revenue is only a recommendation for appropriations and the fund also depends on appropriated amounts.

drawbacks.text: The fund depends on appropriations and voluntary contributions; the contractor tax itself is only a 'sense of the Senate' recommendation for funding, so the program could cost taxpayers substantial sums if the tax or appropriations fall short [S3].

The bill sets spending and fundraising limits only for candidates who choose to participate; it does not limit independent outside spending, so a participating candidate could face unlimited super PAC spending against them while bound to fund-derived resources [S3].
Participation is voluntary, so candidates who expect to raise more from large donors could opt out and run outside the system [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a small fee on very large federal contracts and a dependence on small donations, in exchange for Senate candidates who do not owe their campaigns to checks of thousands of dollars. The serious weaknesses are the unguaranteed funding stream and the fact that the bill leaves independent outside spending untouched, which could blunt the program in practice. Even with those caveats, the effects on ordinary people run in the direction of cheaper campaigns and less donor dependence.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 24, 2019 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Dick Durbin introduced the bill on July 24, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S5].
Twenty-eight senators cosponsored the bill: 26 Democrats and 2 independents [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the referral [S5].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill expired without ever receiving a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The campaign finance status quo: large donors, super PAC fundraising operations, and federal contractors, whose contributions and contract payments remain untouched, along with incumbent senators who continue to finance campaigns under the existing system.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large donors and the big-money status quo

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the 28 cosponsors was a Democrat or independent; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee never considered the bill.

industries.note: Companies with contracts over $10 million would pay a 0.5% fee on contract payments to fund public financing. These firms are also prominent campaign contributors, so the fee and the reduced donor dependence both cut against their influence.

industries.industry: Large-dollar donors and joint fundraising committees
industries.note: Participating candidates could not accept contributions over $200 or use joint fundraising committees, removing the main high-dollar fundraising channels for Senate races.

Stations must accept vouchers and are guaranteed paying customers for political airtime, entrenching their role as the paid channel for campaign advertising, though they must give participating candidates 80% rates, post rate cards, and allow FCC ad-purchase reporting.
